https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-alliance.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LVsP In 2024, hundreds of thousands across the country rallied in protest against right-wing extremism Image: Stefan Boness/IPON/picture alliance Advertisement Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage. For Felix Pankonin , locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property; his bicycles have been vandalized; and other times he receives threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted. Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony . The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political advisor at DaMOst , the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Yes, says Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years. "We have completely different security protocols now. After 6:00 p.m., no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand." Her work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial. Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic society Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance In Saxony-Anhalt , a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities. Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities Miriam Zeller, a councilwoman in Stendal (a city of 37,000 in Saxony-Anhalt), is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the state election on September 6. Zeller told DW that the hostility was even more intense when the Greens were in power. Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia. "It can't get any worse than this," says Zeller. However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job. For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real. Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, is feeling the impact of the shift to the right in her private life as well Image: Miriam Zeller Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves People like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller need more protection. The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists. The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying. Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace. Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over five million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear. "This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works." That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader calls for more commitment from politicians. "We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," Fahimi told DW. Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Hope for help for queer people following the Berlin attack "Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," says Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association (LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people ( LGBTQ+ ) since 1990. "Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann said in an interview with DW. The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlin has deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now of all times. The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, says Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace. "That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl argues. Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas? Felix Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas. Green Party politician Miriam Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas. Andre Lehmann sounds determined: "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he says. This article was translated from German. https://www.dw.com/en/cyberattack-in-ber.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MOxJ After a failed extortion attempt, hackers published 1.4 million records from the Berlin administration Image: picture alliance/dpa Advertisement It was a story that almost went unnoticed amid all the clamor surrounding the closely watched state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. This highly alarming story is one of many recent reports that have detailed attacks on infrastructure or drone attacks on airports carried out by hostile foreign powers. Incidents like this one in the German capital highlight just how vulnerable Germany's data networks are. So what exactly happened? Since early September, employee files, official correspondence, pay stubs and even scanned ID documents have been appearing on the dark web. The hacker group Rhysida stole the data and then tried to extort the Berlin city government. They demanded a ransom of 30 bitcoins, which is equivalent to about €2 million ($2.3 million), or else they would publish the sensitive data. But last Friday, Berlin's Governing Mayor Kai Wegner stated: "The State of Berlin will not give in to blackmail." The data was subsequently published on the dark web, the part of the internet accessible only to tech-savvy users, where a lot of illegal activity takes place. In total, the data set consists of approximately 1.4 million records. Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video An employee unknowingly opened a phishing email Two departments of the city government serving approximately four million residents have been compromised: the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transportation. This time, the attack wasn't carried out by foreign intelligence agencies, but by criminals. The hackers initially gained access to protected data between August 7 and 14 without being detected. Rhysida, a cybercrime group believed to originate from eastern Europe, has been attacking public institutions around the world since 2023, claiming responsibility for nearly 280 attacks, primarily in the US. The hackers were able to gain access when a Berlin Transportation Authority employee replied to a phishing email, a message disguised to appear genuine and benign. Opening one of the attachments inadvertently grants the attackers access to the victim's network. In Berlin, the state government's secure fiber-optic network connects approximately 600 locations, ranging from municipal offices to senate departments. Data disclosure could have serious consequences The list of sectors that experts believe could be compromised illustrates the real gravity of the data breach. In addition to the personal data of employees and citizens, this includes information on combi-heat and power plants, fuel storage facilities, emergency power supply systems as well as prisons and water treatment plants. In an interview with the Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper, Jochim Selzer of the Chaos Computer Club said that the publication could have serious consequences for the people affected — even if the data only appeared on the hard-to-access dark web: "The more you know about a person, the better you can impersonate them and the better you can figure out what you need to know about them in order to, say, place an order on their behalf." As cyberattacks threaten Germany, can Berlin keep data safe? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is changing passwords enough? And what about the political authorities responsible? The Berlin state government has instructed its employees to change their passwords. That, however, sparked outrage from Thorsten Schleheider, the vice-chairman of Berlin's police union. He said that Berlin's data has been inadequately protected for years and that many employees have not received sufficient training: "It is unthinkable that highly sensitive data was compromised for days, and the only action taken appears to be instructing employees to change their passwords." To address the data breach, the Berlin Senate has set up a coordination office involving all Berlin administrative agencies. It has also established contact with federal agencies such as the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), based in Bonn. Mayor Kai Wegner said, "We will inform, advise and support those employees and Berliners who were affected as quickly as possible." Berlin state elections on September 20 remain safe The Berlin authorities were, however, able to provide reassurance regarding at least one issue of concern. They announced that the September 20 election for the Berlin State Parliament is not at risk. State Election Commissioner Stephan Bröchler told the Bild tabloid: "As things stand, all systems and processes necessary for the election remain unaffected — including election preparations, the actual election day itself and the steps leading up to the release of the preliminary results." Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was at least indirectly affected by the data theft. The stolen information also includes details about the controversial expansion of the Chancellery in the heart of Berlin. This article was translated from German.
